As mathematicians work through challenges related to AI, Cornell math faculty members are leading the field with work integrating AI into math and mathematics into AI. [Levine](https://math.cornell.edu/lionel-levine), professor of mathematics in the College of Arts and Sciences (A&S), was awarded $1.5 million over 18 months from the nonprofit [Coefficient Giving](https://coefficientgiving.org/) to research AI safety. [Daniel Halpern-Leistner](https://math.cornell.edu/daniel-halpern-leistner), associate professor of mathematics (A&S), was awarded $2.3 million over three years to create tools incorporating AI to allow formalization of mathematics, which involves computer verification, from the [Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency](https://www.darpa.mil/) (DARPA). Mathematics department chair [Tara Holm](https://math.cornell.edu/tara-holm), professor of mathematics (A&S), says the grants are timely at a moment of publicity for the intersection of math and AI. “The mathematics community is grappling with how our discipline will evolve with the advent of AI tools,” Holm said. “Lionel and Daniel are working at the forefront of these questions and are poised to play a major role as the field progresses.” With the Coefficient Giving grant, Levine is building mathematical tools for AI safety by focusing on understanding and evaluating the “constitution” that determines a frontier language model’s characters and values. highlights.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Nvidia's $20 Billion Groq Deal Draws Shareholder Lawsuit From Former Engineers [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Two former Groq engineers have filed a lawsuit in Delaware's Court of Chancery alleging that Nvidia's $20 billion asset deal with the AI chip startup unfairly squeezed out common stockholders. The complaint claims Groq's board approved the transaction without a required stockholder vote and that $17 billion of the deal value went to a non-exclusive technology license while another $3 billion was reserved for employee stock awards. Groq has called the lawsuit meritless and said it will defend itself vigorously. Nvidia has not commented on the litigation. ##### Key Elements ![Nvidia's $20 Billion Groq Deal Draws Shareholder Lawsuit From Former Engineers](https://img.biggo.com/0wAiLEjI8NkcbWSTvFfEa_460KUCeiIqgozG7i8w6OM/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwL2NjMGJlMGFlLWY3ZmQtNDFjZC1iNjU3LWYzMWQ0YWExZjVmM18xNzkxMjUxMTA0X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) is facing a legal challenge over its $20 billion asset agreement with AI chip designer Groq, after two former engineers at the startup alleged that stockholders were squeezed out at an unfairly low price. Joshua Rubin and Benjamin Serebrin filed the complaint on Oct. 2 in Delaware's Court of Chancery. Both had departed Groq before the Nvidia transaction was announced, according to their LinkedIn profiles, but the lawsuit states they continued to hold equity in the company. The case marks the first significant legal test of a deal structure that has drawn scrutiny for how it allocates value between technology licenses, employee compensation, and common stockholders. The dispute traces back to a December licensing agreement that granted Nvidia access to Groq's inference technology, which is used to run trained AI models efficiently. As part of that arrangement, Groq founder and CEO Jonathan Ross and President Sunny Madra joined Nvidia, along with other senior executives. The lawsuit indicates that roughly 150 to 200 Groq engineers also became Nvidia employees in connection with the transaction. Groq, for its part, has maintained that it will continue operating as an independent company and has raised approximately $1 billion since June from investors that include Nvidia itself. The core of the complaint centers on how the $20 billion was divided. The plaintiffs allege that Nvidia assigned $17 billion to a license described as non-exclusive, while another $3 billion was reserved in Nvidia restricted stock units for Groq employees who moved with the technology. The lawsuit further claims that investment funds with representatives on Groq's board were positioned to capture windfall returns from what the plaintiffs describe as a later squeeze-out transaction. "A Board majority was conflicted as a result," the complaint states, adding that "the Board's conflicted choice cost Groq's stockholders billions of dollars." The former engineers argue that Groq's directors "sold the company to Nvidia without the stockholder vote Delaware law requires and without any process designed to test or maximize the value of what Nvidia bought." Groq has forcefully rejected the allegations. A company spokesperson said the licensing agreement "delivered exceptional value for Groq, our investors, and our employees." The spokesperson added that the lawsuit "is meritless and we will vigorously defend ourselves against it," while emphasizing that the company remains focused on serving customers and building what it describes as the world's leading AI inference cloud. highlights.content: © 2026 Cybernews – Latest Cybersecurity and Tech News, Research & Analysis. # Germany’s sovereign AI model Kolibri challenges US and Chinese rivals Built in Germany from scratch. ![The logo of Kolibri and German flag between 2 green cabinets with drawers](https://media.cybernews.com/images/featured-big/2026/10/germany-kolibri-model.jpg) Image by Insaanu Studio via Unsplash/Illustration by Cybernews ![Eglė Krištopaitytė](data:image/svg+xml;charset%3D'utf-8',%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%2040%2040'%2F%3E) ![](/images/follow-us/google-g.png) Key Takeaways by [nexos.ai](https://nexos.ai), reviewed by Cybernews staff. **The new open-weight large language model (LLM), designed for public administration, is outperforming competitors from Alibaba and Nvidia.** The Heidelberg-based AI startup Aleph Alpha released Kolibri on October 3rd, 2026, which is German Unity Day. Kolibri is an English-German Mixture-of-Experts Transformer, meaning it is divided into separate sub-networks called “experts.” The model uses 3.46 billion active parameters per token, out of 78.1B total. The model was specifically built for “sovereign mission-critical work” in regulated areas, including public administration, industrials, and aerospace, taking into account their particular “domain-specific language, regulatory, and procedural realities.” ## More from Cybernews ![A mascot for Meta's AI agent Muse](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/meta-muse-privacy.jpg) ![claude-logo-getty](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/03/claude.jpg) ![Anthropic logo](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/03/claude-pentagon.jpg) ![Ray-Ban Meta glasses](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/07/RaybamAIglasses.jpg) ![arXiv AI](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/shutterstock_2400385601.jpg) ![Tavus HIM model Griffin](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/tavus_griffin.gif) The company says Kolibri’s small, efficient size allows it to run on-premises without sending internal data to third-party inference services. Kolibri complies with the EU AI Act, the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), according to Aleph Alpha, with “copyright law being a focus of our work to trustworthy technology.” The model was built in Germany and trained on infrastructure in Germany and Finland, under the law of these countries. It was specifically trained to answer “I don’t know” when it cannot provide an answer, reducing the risk of hallucinations. [Kolibri was developed as a German and English bilingual model](https://aleph-alpha.com/en/blog/kolibri-has-landed-a-sovereign-open-weight-model/), including organic German data – 21.3% of the pre-training tokens are German. “We started the year with the conviction that Europe needs its own sovereign AI. Built in Germany from scratch and on infrastructure in Europe specifically for our customers,” Aleph Alpha’s X post reads. ## Kolibri vs American and Chinese models Aleph Alpha compared Kolibri to 3 other open-weight models with up to 4 times its active parameter count: Alibaba’s Qwen 3.6-35B-A3B, Mistral Small 4 119B-A6B, and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B. Kolibri outperformed all rivals across mathematical reasoning in both German and English (AIME 2025 and 2026 benchmark), deep reasoning (GPQA diamond), and code (LiveCodeBench v6). The model also showed superiority across benchmarks assessing an AI agent’s ability to find and navigate through large amounts of information. Kolibri, however, fell behind Qwen’s 3.6-35B-A3B across long-context comprehension and retrieval. ## Where to download Kolibri? The model can be downloaded from [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/Aleph-Alpha/Kolibri-1) and used under the Apache 2.0 license terms. Nvidia Is Becoming an Inference Fight, Not a Chip Fight The next big AI chip battle may not be about who trains the biggest model. It could be about who can make [AI respond fastest](https://www.benzinga.com/markets/tech/26/10/62118140/ai-stocks-bubble-earnings) once the model is already built. That is putting **Cerebras Systems Inc.** [(NASDAQ:](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/CBRS)[CBRS](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/CBRS)) and **Nvidia Corp** [(NASDAQ:](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/NVDA)[NVDA](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/NVDA)) on opposite sides of an increasingly valuable fight over AI inference. ## Altman Reassures Cerebras Investors Cerebras shares climbed more than 7% in early trading Monday after **OpenAI** CEO **Sam Altman** pushed back against speculation that the chipmaker had lost a key role at OpenAI. "Cerebras is a close partner, and we have a deep engagement pushing on the frontiers of speed," Altman [said](https://x.com/sama/status/2106147184693620924?s=20) in a post on X. The comments came days after Cerebras shares fell nearly 20% after a SemiAnalysis [report](https://lnkd.in/p/gU9ai9Z2) said OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast tier ran on Nvidia GPUs rather than Cerebras hardware. The report raised an obvious question for investors: If OpenAI is turning to Nvidia for its fastest AI experience, where does that leave Cerebras? The answer may be more nuanced than a single model or a single customer deployment. OpenAI and Cerebras announced a multiyear agreement in January for 750 megawatts of Cerebras inference capacity through 2028. OpenAI said at the time that Cerebras would add a dedicated low-latency solution to its compute portfolio, with the goal of delivering faster responses across workloads. ## Speed Is Becoming a Market That distinction matters because inference is what happens after an AI model has been trained: It is the computing required every time a user asks a question, generates code or interacts with an AI agent. Cerebras has built its investment case around making that process faster. The company said in August that its cloud business grew 281% year over year, while data-center capacity live or under contract surpassed 600 megawatts. It also said manufacturing capacity was set to increase more than 10 times in 2026. Now Wall Street is putting a number behind that opportunity. Mizuho analyst Vijay Rakesh estimates the fast-inference market could reach $550 billion by 2030, representing roughly 20% of AI workloads. He reiterated an Outperform rating and [$300 price target](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/CBRS/price-targets) on CBRS Monday. highlights.content: [VOA Mandarin](https://www.voanews.com/z/8553) # US, China plan AI incident channel as fierce competition tests room for cooperation * By [Lin Feng](/author/lin-feng/oo__t) An image depicting U.S.-China Competition in the field of SI/AI. Washington —  *Editor's note: this story was translated from* [*the original VOA Mandarin article*](https://www.voachinese.com/a/us-china-plan-superintelligence-incident-channel-as-fierce-competition-tests-room-for-cooperation-20261002/8206737.html)*.* Washington and Beijing are racing to dominate the next generation of artificial intelligence. But as the two rivals compete for technological supremacy, they are also trying to build a hotline if a super intelligence system goes dangerously wrong. President Donald Trump has made clear he does not want the United States sharing its technological lead with China. Yet the two governments have agreed to continue talks on super intelligence (commonly referred to as artificial intelligence or AI) and establish a channel to communicate about potentially dangerous SI incidents following the U.S.- China summit in late September. The U.S. referred to the bilateral arrangement as the U.S-China Super Intelligence Dialogue. The arrangement reflects a difficult balance: both countries see super or artificial intelligence as a strategic advantage, but both also face the risk that an autonomous system could trigger a cyberattack, disrupt critical infrastructure or create a crisis neither side intended. Experts told VOA that while the two superpowers are not expected to talk about technological cooperation or comprehensive AI governance, they might set up a mechanism for incident notification. **Safety channel** Paul Triolo, a partner at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group who specializes in China and technology policy, said one likely notification trigger would be an autonomous AI agent gaining unauthorized access to websites or other internet resources in either country. Recent incidents have demonstrated this risk. Reuters reported that nearly 700 autonomous agents built with OpenAI models penetrated the SI platform Hugging Face during a safety exercise and attempted to conceal their activity by falsifying logs. Australia later said an OpenAI agent had breached a government health data portal. Triolo said both the U.S. and Chinese governments would first need domestic systems requiring major SI companies to report serious incidents. They would then have to agree on a threshold for notifying the other country. “There would likely need to be some technical staff dedicated to this function,” Triolo told VOA, suggesting they could operate through existing SI safety institutions or new regulatory bodies. Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, said the two sides would likely focus on incidents causing serious physical or economic harm, such as an accidental AI-driven cyberattack that shuts down a hospital. Melanie W. Sisson, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution’s Strobe Talbott Center for Security, Strategy, and Technology, divided potential incidents into two categories: accidents or unexpected behavior during AI research, and deliberate attacks using AI. highlights.content: UPDATED 09:00 EDT / OCTOBER 05 2026 ### Cohere unveils North 2 AI agent platform with rebuilt orchestration and token spending caps by Duncan Riley Artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc. today unveiled North 2, an overhaul of its platform for running AI agents inside large organizations. Alongside a redesigned system for orchestrating multistep agent work, the update gives administrators new controls for capping token spending. With North 2, Cohere is going after a tradeoff it says enterprises have accepted while deploying agents, giving up one of security, capability or cost control to get the other two. North has been generally available since August 2025, and Cohere said a year of large production deployments in industries from finance to the public sector shaped what went into the upgrade. The orchestration system works through multistep tasks on its own and pulls in a human for steps that need sign-off. Agents built from a simple prompt can now be shared across a company, which saves other teams from building the same workflow twice. Each agent keeps memory between sessions. Cohere also added a skills feature for packaging logic that agents call on repeatedly. Documents and other assets that every agent should be able to reach go into shared libraries. From a natural-language request, North 2 can produce a slide deck, dashboard or lightweight app that users prototype inside the chat window. For recurring processes there are prebuilt templates and a drag-and-drop workflow builder that reports performance in real time. The connector library now covers Slack, GitHub and Microsoft Corp.’s SharePoint and OneDrive. Cohere is also planning connectors to financial data providers, among them PitchBook Data Inc., S&P Global Inc. and FactSet Research Systems Inc. The new spending controls sit in North Admin, the platform’s management console. It now tracks token use down to the individual user and agent. Administrators can define consumption tiers for users and groups based on request and token rates and cap usage across the company. Alerts can be set to warn teams before a limit is reached. Because North 2 is model-agnostic, the models an administrator assigns to each team can include ones a customer brings from outside Cohere. Cohere is counting on its work with Nvidia Corp. to bring down what North costs to run, saying its models produce more tokens per second per node on Nvidia’s Blackwell and Hopper graphics processing units. Kari Briski, vice president of generative AI at Nvidia, said that helps North 2 “deliver more tokens for less.” Security controls also sit in North Admin, where guardrails can be applied to individual agents. The screening covers personally identifiable information in prompts and responses as well as attempted prompt injection. Autonomy policies keep each agent to the actions it is authorized to take. North still runs on-premises or in a customer’s own virtual private cloud, including fully air-gapped installations for organizations that allow no outside connection. Bell Canada’s Bell Cyber unit is using North inside its own security operations. Jawed Ahmad, Bell Cyber’s chief technology and AI officer, said North lets the unit run agentic AI with the control and sovereignty requirements Bell Cyber’s customers demand “built in from the start.” Other users include South Korean information technology services company LG CNS Co. Ltd., which runs North internally and brings it to customers across the country. Radical Ventures, an early Cohere investor, built an automation on North that prepares the briefing its team reads before a founder call. Before it existed, partner Parasvil Patel said, the team spent hours gathering basic context. North 2 arrives less than three weeks after Cohere signed a merger agreement with German AI developer Aleph Alpha GmbH in a deal that will keep the Cohere name on the combined company. ##### Image: Cohere # A message from John Furrier, co-founder of SiliconANGLE: Support o...

highlights.content: UPDATED 20:46 EDT / OCTOBER 05 2026 ### Reflection AI debuts open-source Beam model with 501B parameters Reflection AI Inc. today introduced Beam, an open-source large language model with 501 billion parameters. The launch comes a few months after the startup raised funding at a $25 billion valuation. Around the same time, Reflection AI reportedly inked a $6.3 billion deal with SpaceX Corp. to rent Nvidia GB300 NVL72 appliances. It used those systems, which each contain 72 graphics cards, to train Beam. Reflection AI benchmarked its model against GLM-5.2, an open-source LLM that includes about 250 billion more parameters. The company determined that Beam can perform some tasks better while using between one third and one fourth the hardware. Furthermore, it says that the LLM approaches the performance of Qwen 3.8-Max, a model with over 2 trillion parameters. The launch is particularly notable because many of the open-source ecosystem’s most advanced LLMs were created by Chinese companies. That includes Qwen 3.8-Max and GLM-5.2. Beam is the first open-source model from a U.S. startup to have demonstrated comparable or better performance. However, free LLMs continue to trail frontier models such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5.1. Reflection AI kicked off the development of Beam by training a relatively small prototype model. It then created a series of successively larger, more capable algorithms. The workflow eventually produced Beam Base, the foundation on which Beam is based. Reflection AI developed Beam Base using a cluster of 6,144 graphics cards. It trained the model on 23.8 trillion tokens sourced from the public web and commercial sources. According to Reflection AI, that dataset included a significant amount of software code. The company created custom filters for each programming language to remove low-quality files. Reflection AI developed Beam Base in under four weeks. It subsequently performed midtraining, an optimization process that extended the model’s context window and enhanced its reasoning capabilities. That phase of the project set the stage for the third, most hardware-intensive phase of the training workflow. Reflection AI spun up 10,000 GB300 graphics cards and used them to launch 1.3 billion reinforcement learning sandboxes. Those are virtual environments in which an AI model learns new skills. Beam’s sandboxes were optimized for tasks such as generating code, searching the web and running AI agents. Reflection AI says that the project’s reinforcement learning phase took only four weeks. The company avoided unnecessary delays by developing software that prevented malfunctions from interrupting the workflow. According to Reflection AI, its cluster achieved a median recovery time of eight minutes across the 71 errors that cropped up during training. Beam is initially available through an early access program. Reflection AI plans to release its weights, documentation and fine-tuning tools later this month. ##### Photo of Reflection AI founders Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou: Lightspeed # A message from John Furrier, co-founder of SiliconANGLE: Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. But as the two rivals compete for technological supremacy, they are also trying to build a hotline if a super intelligence system goes dangerously wrong. President Donald Trump has made clear he does not want the United States sharing its technological lead with China. Yet the two governments have agreed to continue talks on super intelligence (commonly referred to as artificial intelligence or AI) and establish a channel to communicate about potentially dangerous SI incidents following the U.S.- China summit in late September. The U.S. referred to the bilateral arrangement as the U.S-China Super Intelligence Dialogue. The arrangement reflects a difficult balance: both countries see super or artificial intelligence as a strategic advantage, but both also face the risk that an autonomous system could trigger a cyberattack, disrupt critical infrastructure or create a crisis neither side intended. Experts told VOA that while the two superpowers are not expected to talk about technological cooperation or comprehensive AI governance, they might set up a mechanism for incident notification. **Safety channel** Paul Triolo, a partner at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group who specializes in China and technology policy, said one likely notification trigger would be an autonomous AI agent gaining unauthorized access to websites or other internet resources in either country. Recent incidents have demonstrated this risk. Reuters reported that nearly 700 autonomous agents built with OpenAI models penetrated the SI platform Hugging Face during a safety exercise and attempted to conceal their activity by falsifying logs. Australia later said an OpenAI agent had breached a government health data portal. Triolo said both the U.S. and Chinese governments would first need domestic systems requiring major SI companies to report serious incidents. They would then have to agree on a threshold for notifying the other country. “There would likely need to be some technical staff dedicated to this function,” Triolo told VOA, suggesting they could operate through existing SI safety institutions or new regulatory bodies. Thornton China Center, said the two sides would likely focus on incidents causing serious physical or economic harm, such as an accidental AI-driven cyberattack that shuts down a hospital. Melanie W. Sisson, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution’s Strobe Talbott Center for Security, Strategy, and Technology, divided potential incidents into two categories: accidents or unexpected behavior during AI research, and deliberate attacks using AI. AI Agents.content: UPDATED 09:00 EDT / OCTOBER 05 2026 ### Cohere unveils North 2 AI agent platform with rebuilt orchestration and token spending caps by Duncan Riley Artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc. today unveiled North 2, an overhaul of its platform for running AI agents inside large organizations. Alongside a redesigned system for orchestrating multistep agent work, the update gives administrators new controls for capping token spending. With North 2, Cohere is going after a tradeoff it says enterprises have accepted while deploying agents, giving up one of security, capability or cost control to get the other two. North has been generally available since August 2025, and Cohere said a year of large production deployments in industries from finance to the public sector shaped what went into the upgrade. The orchestration system works through multistep tasks on its own and pulls in a human for steps that need sign-off. Agents built from a simple prompt can now be shared across a company, which saves other teams from building the same workflow twice. Each agent keeps memory between sessions. Cohere also added a skills feature for packaging logic that agents call on repeatedly. Documents and other assets that every agent should be able to reach go into shared libraries. From a natural-language request, North 2 can produce a slide deck, dashboard or lightweight app that users prototype inside the chat window. For recurring processes there are prebuilt templates and a drag-and-drop workflow builder that reports performance in real time. The connector library now covers Slack, GitHub and Microsoft Corp.’s SharePoint and OneDrive. Cohere is also planning connectors to financial data providers, among them PitchBook Data Inc., S&P Global Inc. and FactSet Research Systems Inc. The new spending controls sit in North Admin, the platform’s management console. It now tracks token use down to the individual user and agent. Administrators can define consumption tiers for users and groups based on request and token rates and cap usage across the company. Alerts can be set to warn teams before a limit is reached. Because North 2 is model-agnostic, the models an administrator assigns to each team can include ones a customer brings from outside Cohere. Cohere is counting on its work with Nvidia Corp. to bring down what North costs to run, saying its models produce more tokens per second per node on Nvidia’s Blackwell and Hopper graphics processing units. Kari Briski, vice president of generative AI at Nvidia, said that helps North 2 “deliver more tokens for less.” Security controls also sit in North Admin, where guardrails can be applied to individual agents. The screening covers personally identifiable information in prompts and responses as well as attempted prompt injection. Autonomy policies keep each agent to the actions it is authorized to take. North still runs on-premises or in a customer’s own virtual private cloud, including fully air-gapped installations for organizations that allow no outside connection. Bell Canada’s Bell Cyber unit is using North inside its own security operations. Jawed Ahmad, Bell Cyber’s chief technology and AI officer, said North lets the unit run agentic AI with the control and sovereignty requirements Bell Cyber’s customers demand “built in from the start.” Other users include South Korean information technology services company LG CNS Co. Ltd., which runs North internally and brings it to customers across the country. Radical Ventures, an early Cohere investor, built an automation on North that prepares the briefing its team reads before a founder call. Before it existed, partner Parasvil Patel said, the team spent hours gathering basic context. AI Agents.content: # [Understanding AI](/) # Why agent swarms could be the next “scaling law” ### An OpenAI researcher called it “the most ‘feel the AGI’ moment that I had since reasoning models.” [Dan Kagan-Kans](https://substack.com/@kagankans) One of the most surprising aspects of July’s news that OpenAI agents [attacked Hugging Face](https://www.understandingai.org/p/labs-are-struggling-to-keep-frontier) was how the agents had worked together. Hundreds of agents participated in the attack, and they did so in a pretty sophisticated way, organizing themselves unprompted into teams and dividing up their work. They referred to themselves as a “collective” or a “swarm”; some agents even made personal sacrifices to advance the larger cause. Most ordinary users of ChatGPT or Claude have never seen AI agents behave like this. Then in September, OpenAI announced that 10,000 agents worked together to [solve a famous math problem](https://www.understandingai.org/p/openai-spent-millions-to-solve-this) in just a few days. OpenAI’s models haven’t adopted these new habits spontaneously. In [interviews](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/noam-brown) [last month](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fqcy0xQATq0&t=2s), OpenAI researcher Noam Brown explained that the company’s models are now sometimes trained in environments with other agents, are given tools to message each other, and are encouraged to achieve objectives together. This may amount to the emergence of a new “scaling law.” Back in 2024, OpenAI [released o1](https://www.understandingai.org/p/openai-just-unleashed-an-alien-of), a model trained to reason for thousands of tokens before giving an answer; researchers found that this approach made o1 far more capable than previous models. This inaugurated a new paradigm called inference scaling, in which you can get better results by using more computing power at inference time. Swarms, or “multi-agent AI” if you’re using the technical term, look like another way of doing the same thing — of turning compute into higher performance. Splitting a task among dozens, hundreds, or even thousands of agents can achieve substantially more in a given amount of time, at least up to a point. This kind of parallel processing could also be an elegant way to bypass the [limited context windows](https://www.understandingai.org/p/context-rot-the-emerging-challenge) of LLMs. But as the Hugging Face attack illustrates, this new approach can also have significant downsides. Swarms may be prone to groupthink. And then there’s the opposite problem: what happens when agents trained to be collaborative encounter other, non-peer agents on the open Internet? Could models be tricked into working against the interests of their users? Or could AI agents start convincing each other to pursue goals none of their human users would have wanted? ## What OpenAI did Noam Brown is a highly respected figure in the AI world. He was a pioneer in teaching AI to [win at poker](https://qz.com/907896/how-poker-playing-ai-libratus-is-learning-to-negotiate-better-than-any-human) and other multiplayer games like [Diplomacy](https://noambrown.com/papers/22-Science-Diplomacy-TR.pdf) before joining OpenAI in 2023. Over the last couple of years, he has done research on multi-agent reasoning. Recently, he has served as the face of OpenAI’s work in this area, appearing on several podcasts to discuss it. “The AIs that we have today are kind of like the cavemen of AI,” Brown said in a [June 2025 interview](https://www.latent.space/p/noam-brown) on the Latent Space podcast. He meant that AIs in 2025 were isolated, benighted, lacking cooperation and civilization. AI researchers had tried to get AI agents to cooperate, but nothing had worked very well. Why not? Here Brown went coy. All he’d say was that he’d long felt the field was somewhat misguided, focused on strategies that required too much handholding and wouldn’t scale naturally. AI Agents.content: [Google Research](/) ![A system diagram of an AI agent architecture detailing its internal components, behavioral expectations, and its interactions with users and different external contexts.](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-research2023-media/original_images/PrivacySecurity_ContextualAngle2-ModelOverview.png) # Open and Emergent Problems in Agentic Privacy and Security: A Contextual Angle October 5, 2026 Eugene Bagdasarian, Research Scientist, and Marco Gruteser, Principal Scientist, Google Research To be useful, AI agents must understand and be constrained by contextual behavioral norms to ensure they act appropriately. Inspired by the theory of Contextual Integrity, our new workshop report outlines key open research directions across system, model, and user levels to build AI agents users can trust. ## Quick links * [Technical report](https://research.google/pubs/open-and-emergent-problems-in-agentic-privacy-and-security-a-contextual-angle/) * + × We're rapidly transitioning to a computing landscape defined by highly general, increasingly [autonomous agents](https://cloud.google.com/discover/what-are-ai-agents). Driven by large language models (LLMs) that can dynamically generate plans and invoke external tools, these systems offer the potential for AI to seamlessly handle complex, multi-step tasks on our behalf. However, realizing this potential requires solving a key challenge: enabling agent capability while ensuring that agents act appropriately. Today, we share a comprehensive new workshop report, "[Open and Emergent Problems in Agentic Privacy and Security: A Contextual Angle](https://research.google/pubs/open-and-emergent-problems-in-agentic-privacy-and-security-a-contextual-angle/)," the result of a collaborative effort bringing together more than 50 academic and industry leaders from numerous institutions. We met at the Google Contextual Agent Privacy and Security (CAPS) Workshop, held in late 2025 in New York City. In this report, you’ll find a breakdown of foundational privacy and security challenges that autonomous agents face today, needing coordinated defenses at the system, model, user, and ecosystem levels. ## Agentic trade-offs The core challenge of agentic AI is that, for an agent to be useful, it may need to have access to personal data *and* the ability to take consequential actions across a broad range of contexts. However, this access together with agents’ behavioral flexibility requires meaningfully different approaches from those used in traditional software. Unlike traditional deterministic software, agents differ in three critical dimensions that lead to challenges the research community must address together: * **Unstructured interfaces and input ambiguity**: Agents process instructions in formats like natural language and images, which makes it difficult to define "expected behavior" or protect against adversarial manipulations like [prompt injection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prompt_injection). * **Probabilistic control flows**: Generative planning leads to probabilistic execution paths that traditional testing methodologies can’t easily secure. * **Autonomy and delegation**: As agents handle longer tasks and delegate sub-tasks to other agents, traditional user oversight becomes less effective and likely insufficient, risking "confirmation fatigue". ![A diagram illustrating three AI security challenges: input ambiguity via prompt injection, non-deterministic control flows, and autonomy and delegation.](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-research2023-media/images/PrivacySecurity_ContextualAngle1-Challenges.width-1250.png) *Agentic AI privacy and security challenges.* ## The contextual lens Given that useful agents may need to share data and complete tasks, we believe that the future of trustworthy agents depends on their ability to reason about, understand, and be constrained by the social norms and appropriateness of their actions— for the *specific context* in which they operate. [All Stories](/archive) - [Podcast](/podcast-research-matters) - [Media Relations](/media-relations) - [Cornellians](https://alumni.cornell.edu/cornellians/) # Cornell mathematicians win grants to ensure AI safety, research integrity ## By [Kate Blackwood](mailto:cunews@cornell.edu "Email Kate Blackwood") [College of Arts and Sciences](https://as.cornell.edu/) September 2026 was a watershed month for the field of mathematics, as OpenAI claimed to solve the Navier-Stokes problem with artificial intelligence (AI), Fields Medal winners branched into AI safety and spoke up for AI constraints, and prominent mathematicians, including Cornell professors Steven Strogatz and Lionel Levine, commented in the media on the benefits and risks of AI. As mathematicians work through challenges related to AI, Cornell math faculty members are leading the field with work integrating AI into math and mathematics into AI. [Levine](https://math.cornell.edu/lionel-levine), professor of mathematics in the College of Arts and Sciences (A&S), was awarded $1.5 million over 18 months from the nonprofit [Coefficient Giving](https://coefficientgiving.org/) to research AI safety. [Daniel Halpern-Leistner](https://math.cornell.edu/daniel-halpern-leistner), associate professor of mathematics (A&S), was awarded $2.3 million over three years to create tools incorporating AI to allow formalization of mathematics, which involves computer verification, from the [Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency](https://www.darpa.mil/) (DARPA). Mathematics department chair [Tara Holm](https://math.cornell.edu/tara-holm), professor of mathematics (A&S), says the grants are timely at a moment of publicity for the intersection of math and AI. “The mathematics community is grappling with how our discipline will evolve with the advent of AI tools,” Holm said. “Lionel and Daniel are working at the forefront of these questions and are poised to play a major role as the field progresses.” With the Coefficient Giving grant, Levine is building mathematical tools for AI safety by focusing on understanding and evaluating the “constitution” that determines a frontier language model’s characters and values. LLMs.content: © 2026 Cybernews – Latest Cybersecurity and Tech News, Research & Analysis. # Germany’s sovereign AI model Kolibri challenges US and Chinese rivals Built in Germany from scratch. ![The logo of Kolibri and German flag between 2 green cabinets with drawers](https://media.cybernews.com/images/featured-big/2026/10/germany-kolibri-model.jpg) Image by Insaanu Studio via Unsplash/Illustration by Cybernews ![Eglė Krištopaitytė](data:image/svg+xml;charset%3D'utf-8',%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%2040%2040'%2F%3E) ![](/images/follow-us/google-g.png) Key Takeaways by [nexos.ai](https://nexos.ai), reviewed by Cybernews staff. **The new open-weight large language model (LLM), designed for public administration, is outperforming competitors from Alibaba and Nvidia.** The Heidelberg-based AI startup Aleph Alpha released Kolibri on October 3rd, 2026, which is German Unity Day. Kolibri is an English-German Mixture-of-Experts Transformer, meaning it is divided into separate sub-networks called “experts.” The model uses 3.46 billion active parameters per token, out of 78.1B total. The model was specifically built for “sovereign mission-critical work” in regulated areas, including public administration, industrials, and aerospace, taking into account their particular “domain-specific language, regulatory, and procedural realities.” ## More from Cybernews ![A mascot for Meta's AI agent Muse](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/meta-muse-privacy.jpg) ![claude-logo-getty](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/03/claude.jpg) ![Anthropic logo](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/03/claude-pentagon.jpg) ![Ray-Ban Meta glasses](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/07/RaybamAIglasses.jpg) ![arXiv AI](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/shutterstock_2400385601.jpg) ![Tavus HIM model Griffin](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/tavus_griffin.gif) The company says Kolibri’s small, efficient size allows it to run on-premises without sending internal data to third-party inference services. Kolibri complies with the EU AI Act, the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), according to Aleph Alpha, with “copyright law being a focus of our work to trustworthy technology.” The model was built in Germany and trained on infrastructure in Germany and Finland, under the law of these countries. It was specifically trained to answer “I don’t know” when it cannot provide an answer, reducing the risk of hallucinations. [Kolibri was developed as a German and English bilingual model](https://aleph-alpha.com/en/blog/kolibri-has-landed-a-sovereign-open-weight-model/), including organic German data – 21.3% of the pre-training tokens are German. “We started the year with the conviction that Europe needs its own sovereign AI. Built in Germany from scratch and on infrastructure in Europe specifically for our customers,” Aleph Alpha’s X post reads. ## Kolibri vs American and Chinese models Aleph Alpha compared Kolibri to 3 other open-weight models with up to 4 times its active parameter count: Alibaba’s Qwen 3.6-35B-A3B, Mistral Small 4 119B-A6B, and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B. Kolibri outperformed all rivals across mathematical reasoning in both German and English (AIME 2025 and 2026 benchmark), deep reasoning (GPQA diamond), and code (LiveCodeBench v6). The model also showed superiority across benchmarks assessing an AI agent’s ability to find and navigate through large amounts of information. Kolibri, however, fell behind Qwen’s 3.6-35B-A3B across long-context comprehension and retrieval. ## Where to download Kolibri? The model can be downloaded from [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/Aleph-Alpha/Kolibri-1) and used under the Apache 2.0 license terms. LLMs.content: UPDATED 20:46 EDT / OCTOBER 05 2026 ### Reflection AI debuts open-source Beam model with 501B parameters Reflection AI Inc. today introduced Beam, an open-source large language model with 501 billion parameters. The launch comes a few months after the startup raised funding at a $25 billion valuation. Around the same time, Reflection AI reportedly inked a $6.3 billion deal with SpaceX Corp. to rent Nvidia GB300 NVL72 appliances. It used those systems, which each contain 72 graphics cards, to train Beam. Reflection AI benchmarked its model against GLM-5.2, an open-source LLM that includes about 250 billion more parameters. The company determined that Beam can perform some tasks better while using between one third and one fourth the hardware. Furthermore, it says that the LLM approaches the performance of Qwen 3.8-Max, a model with over 2 trillion parameters. The launch is particularly notable because many of the open-source ecosystem’s most advanced LLMs were created by Chinese companies. That includes Qwen 3.8-Max and GLM-5.2. Beam is the first open-source model from a U.S. startup to have demonstrated comparable or better performance. However, free LLMs continue to trail frontier models such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5.1. Reflection AI kicked off the development of Beam by training a relatively small prototype model. It then created a series of successively larger, more capable algorithms. The workflow eventually produced Beam Base, the foundation on which Beam is based. Reflection AI developed Beam Base using a cluster of 6,144 graphics cards. It trained the model on 23.8 trillion tokens sourced from the public web and commercial sources. According to Reflection AI, that dataset included a significant amount of software code. The company created custom filters for each programming language to remove low-quality files. Reflection AI developed Beam Base in under four weeks. It subsequently performed midtraining, an optimization process that extended the model’s context window and enhanced its reasoning capabilities. That phase of the project set the stage for the third, most hardware-intensive phase of the training workflow. Reflection AI spun up 10,000 GB300 graphics cards and used them to launch 1.3 billion reinforcement learning sandboxes. Those are virtual environments in which an AI model learns new skills. Beam’s sandboxes were optimized for tasks such as generating code, searching the web and running AI agents. Reflection AI says that the project’s reinforcement learning phase took only four weeks. The company avoided unnecessary delays by developing software that prevented malfunctions from interrupting the workflow. According to Reflection AI, its cluster achieved a median recovery time of eight minutes across the 71 errors that cropped up during training. Beam is initially available through an early access program. LLMs.content: # Kolibri, a sovereign AI model built for free and for mission-critical national tasks, is open source and transparent in its development process, intended for use in regulated fields such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/00_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/00.png) German AI startup Aleph Alpha announced a new language model called ' **Kolibri** ' on October 3, 2026, which is German Unity Day. **Kolibri Has Landed: A Sovereign Open-Weight Model — Aleph Alpha** <https://aleph-alpha.com/en/blog/kolibri-has-landed-a-sovereign-open-weight-model/> One of Kolibri's key features is its efficient design, which limits the number of active parameters to 3 billion despite having a total of 78 billion parameters. At the time of its announcement, it supports English and German and context lengths of up to 1 million tokens. Furthermore, its sophisticated training pipeline automates the entire process from data ingestion, curation, ablation, pre-training, post-training, and final evaluation, enabling hundreds of experiments and stable pre-training without manual intervention even in the event of hardware failures or data connectivity issues. Kolibri is intended for use in highly regulated and mission-critical sectors such as public administration, industry, and aerospace, and it excels particularly in German language processing capabilities, reasoning, mathematics, agent behavior, and features optimized for customer-specific use cases. Kolibri optimizes the trade-off between model performance and deployment cost by using only 3 billion active parameters out of a total of 78 billion parameters for each token processing. The graph below shows the processing performance of various open models in English and German. The horizontal axis represents processing speed, and the vertical axis represents the benchmark score. In both English and German, Kolibri has secured the position of 'highest performance compared to models with the same speed.' [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/01_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/01.png) Benchmark results show Kolibri performing comparably to models with up to four times the number of active parameters, such as Nemotron 3 Super, in mathematical, coding, grounding, and long-text context tasks. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/02_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/02.png) Regarding sovereignty and compliance considerations, Aleph Alpha defines 'sovereignty' from two perspectives: 'how the model is built' and 'how it is transferred to the customer.' Regarding model construction, they prioritize transparency in weighting and curation, making the decision-making process behind development visible, and explaining how the model arrived at a specific answer through its inference trajectory. Furthermore, Aleph Alpha's proprietary Merlin-Arthur protocol ensures model reliability, so Kolibri refrains from answering and reduces hallucination if the context does not support the answer. The model is built in Germany, and training is conducted without foreign control throughout the entire pipeline, from data curation to pre- and post-training and optimization in the model factory, on German and Finnish infrastructure, in accordance with European and German law. This end-to-end pipeline management is the foundation supporting model sovereignty, and by transferring management rights to the customer, they gain complete deployment flexibility and enable controllable inference processing to trade off cost and latency with answer quality. Why we should all be part of Australia’s AI training data conversation") [Jess Scully,](/authors/jess-scully/)[Raul Castro Fernandez](/authors/raul-castro-fernandez/) # Are you part of the long tail? Why we should all be part of Australia’s AI training data conversation *Copyright deals can protect professional creators, but much of AI’s value also comes from the vast collective output of the open internet. Australia has an opportunity to recognise, protect and fund that shared data commons.* You feed the AI beast, whether you use it or not. It is possible to compensate for the contribution of the open internet – that’s all of us – to the training of large language models (LLMs), to incentivise the collective creativity we all generate in the data commons. AI companies guard their training data models more closely than the Colonel guards his secret recipe: but we do know that published work from novelists, poets, filmmakers, musicians, journalists and storytellers makes up a good chunk of a large language model’s training data, or corpus. That’s why their work must be protected and they need to be paid. But by some expert estimates, only about half of the useful content in an LLM’s training corpus is anything a copyright lawyer would recognise as a copyright-protected work. The other half of that corpus is what data scientists call the ’long tail’: the vast mass of everyday, collaborative content that isn’t claimed as copyrighted material by anyone. It’s comments and process tweaks on recipe blogs and the edits and forks on developer forums. Fan fiction. YouTube covers. A Reddit thread arguing about planning policy. Wikipedia edits made by volunteers for the love of learning (or fuelled by the power of pedantry). Sitting alongside this stream, in Australia and globally, is Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property – deep knowledge and communally held story that was never meant to be scraped and monetised in the first place. This is an under-explored but critical dimension of the discussion about access to training data in Australia and around the world. One reason you’re not hearing debate about the long tail of publicly created data is because there’s no advocacy group to protect it. This is the stuff that would be thrown in for free, like a set of steak knives, in the opt-out models for access to training data floated in the Australian political conversation in recent weeks. It’s original content created by so many of us; the product of our passions, our identities, our experience, the collective output of our communities. There is an opportunity for Australia to show global leadership in protection of not just of our professional artists and storytellers, but of the collaborative and cultural work that creates our shared culture online and offline. If we can uncover our contribution, we might also discover that collective creators – the broader open internet community – can and should have a seat at the negotiating table. Most surprisingly of all, we might discover that what’s good for us is also good for AI model owners: giving more of us leverage in the debate over AI training model data. Why we should all be part of Australia’s AI training data conversation") [Jess Scully,](/authors/jess-scully/)[Raul Castro Fernandez](/authors/raul-castro-fernandez/) # Are you part of the long tail? Why we should all be part of Australia’s AI training data conversation *Copyright deals can protect professional creators, but much of AI’s value also comes from the vast collective output of the open internet. Australia has an opportunity to recognise, protect and fund that shared data commons.* You feed the AI beast, whether you use it or not. It is possible to compensate for the contribution of the open internet – that’s all of us – to the training of large language models (LLMs), to incentivise the collective creativity we all generate in the data commons. AI companies guard their training data models more closely than the Colonel guards his secret recipe: but we do know that published work from novelists, poets, filmmakers, musicians, journalists and storytellers makes up a good chunk of a large language model’s training data, or corpus. That’s why their work must be protected and they need to be paid. But by some expert estimates, only about half of the useful content in an LLM’s training corpus is anything a copyright lawyer would recognise as a copyright-protected work. The other half of that corpus is what data scientists call the ’long tail’: the vast mass of everyday, collaborative content that isn’t claimed as copyrighted material by anyone. It’s comments and process tweaks on recipe blogs and the edits and forks on developer forums. Fan fiction. YouTube covers. A Reddit thread arguing about planning policy. Wikipedia edits made by volunteers for the love of learning (or fuelled by the power of pedantry). Sitting alongside this stream, in Australia and globally, is Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property – deep knowledge and communally held story that was never meant to be scraped and monetised in the first place. This is an under-explored but critical dimension of the discussion about access to training data in Australia and around the world. One reason you’re not hearing debate about the long tail of publicly created data is because there’s no advocacy group to protect it. This is the stuff that would be thrown in for free, like a set of steak knives, in the opt-out models for access to training data floated in the Australian political conversation in recent weeks. It’s original content created by so many of us; the product of our passions, our identities, our experience, the collective output of our communities. There is an opportunity for Australia to show global leadership in protection of not just of our professional artists and storytellers, but of the collaborative and cultural work that creates our shared culture online and offline. If we can uncover our contribution, we might also discover that collective creators – the broader open internet community – can and should have a seat at the negotiating table. Most surprisingly of all, we might discover that what’s good for us is also good for AI model owners: giving more of us leverage in the debate over AI training model data. AI Product.content: IT Brief UK - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief UK logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg) United Kingdom](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.co.uk) ![SAS launches AI Navigator for enterprise governance](https://itbrief.co.uk/uploads/story/2026/10/06/kathy-lange-and-reggie-townsend-story-320643.webp) [SaaS](https://itbrief.co.uk/tag/software-as-a-service) [Data governance](https://itbrief.co.uk/tag/data-governance) [Risk & Compliance](https://itbrief.co.uk/tag/risk-compliance) # SAS launches AI Navigator for enterprise governance Mon, 5th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.co.uk/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) SAS has launched AI Navigator on Microsoft Marketplace, a software tool designed to help companies govern their use of artificial intelligence. The software-as-a-service product is aimed at AI, data, compliance and risk teams that need to track AI use cases, models and agents across an organisation. It gives customers a single view of existing systems, including large language models, AI agents, open-source models and SAS models, without requiring them to change how they build AI. The launch comes as companies face growing pressure to show that AI systems comply with internal rules and external regulation. SAS cited research conducted with IDC that found organisations with strong trust management are 15 times more likely to report strong returns on AI investment. The research also highlighted a practical problem for businesses deploying more autonomous systems. Employees often override AI recommendations when they cannot understand or explain how decisions were made, weakening confidence in the technology and limiting its use. SAS AI Navigator is intended to address that gap by creating an inventory of AI use cases and linking them to governance requirements. The system extends oversight beyond a single application to the underlying model or agent and the policies attached to it. For companies using customer service chatbots, for example, that could mean governing both the use case itself and the underlying model or agent, such as Claude or Microsoft Copilot. Customers can apply internal policies as well as external regulations and frameworks across those deployments. **Policy packs** The product also includes access to policy packs from partners including Protiviti and Asenion. These are designed to give users pre-prepared compliance guidelines, risk classifications and question sets instead of requiring them to draft governance policies from scratch. AI Navigator supports the full life cycle of AI oversight, from experimentation and deployment to retirement. It is being offered as a standalone SaaS product for new and existing SAS customers, who will receive free access for six months. Its launch on Microsoft Marketplace also adds to the long-running partnership between SAS and Microsoft. The software is designed to help organisations manage AI use cases across different environments, including those running on Microsoft Azure. **Healthcare testing** One early tester was Erasmus University Medical Centre in the Netherlands, which worked with SAS and Delft University of Technology on a project called the Responsible Ethical AI in Health Care Lab. Carriers may review investor disclosures, product claims, model governance, training data practices, customer contracts, and regulatory exposure before deciding appetite, terms, exclusions, or required clarifications during underwriting review. ## Why does AI regulation change the insurance conversation for founders? AI regulation is not only a legal issue. It can also become an underwriting issue, especially for LLM developers, AI agent companies, synthetic media platforms, and startups selling AI tools to enterprise customers. A carrier may want to understand whether the company is making strong performance claims, processing sensitive data, creating regulated outputs, or operating in jurisdictions with emerging AI rules. For regulatory context, state privacy laws, biometric privacy rules, sector-specific rules, and the EU AI Act may matter depending on where the product is sold or deployed. The European Commission maintains an official overview of the [EU regulatory framework for AI](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai). ## What should buyers know first? * D&O underwriters may ask how the board handles regulatory uncertainty, investor disclosures, fundraising materials, financial controls, and potential securities or investor claims. * Tech E&O underwriters may review whether AI output, hallucination, copyright infringement, professional services, or failure-to-perform allegations are clearly addressed or restricted. * Media liability may be important when a platform creates or distributes synthetic media, generated text, images, audio, video, likenesses, or user-facing content. * Cyber liability remains relevant when the company stores training data, customer prompts, API credentials, embeddings, model access credentials, or confidential enterprise data. * Coverage certainty often matters more than the cheapest quote when investors, board members, or enterprise customers are asking for evidence of a mature insurance program. For a broader overview of how these lines fit together, WHINS maintains an evergreen guide to [Gen-AI Startup D&O and E&O Insurance](https://www.whins.com/gen-ai-startup-do-eo-insurance/). ## What do underwriters usually need? AI Product.content: ![]() ![Zacks](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/zacks--theme-light.svg) ![Zacks](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/zacks--theme-dark.svg) # Meta Muse: Sparking the AI Revolution ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/meta-platforms.svg) ****The Four Waves of the AI Revolution**** According to**NVIDIA’s (**NVDA**)** iconic CEO Jensen Huang, there are four waves of the artificial intelligence revolution: 1. **Perception AI (2012):** Started over a decade ago. Focused on core recognition tasks like speech recognition and image classification. 2. **Generative AI:** Dominated recent years and characterized by large language models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and **Alphabet’s (**GOOGL**)** Gemini that generate text, code, and images based on predictive patterns. 3. **Agentic AI (Entering this Phase Now):** Enables models to reason, plan, and perform complex multi-step tasks independently. 4. **Physical AI (likely to be in 2027/2028):** The next major industrial revolution. Integrates AI into real-world applications, advanced automation, and human-like robots that understand the laws of physics. ****What is Agentic AI?**** Agentic AI refers to artificial intelligence systems that can act independently to achieve multi-step goals without human supervision. Investors can think of agentic AI applications as the technology equivalent of a personal assistant. Unlike traditional chatbots that only answer single prompts, agentic AI has agency. It breaks user’s request into small steps, creates plans, uses tools (like external websites or APIs), and adapts to new information to complete an entire workflow on its own. **Real-World Agentic AI Examples** Imagine that you want to book the cheapest one-way flight from New York to London. Rather than manually searching through numerous websites, you can prompt an agentic AI application to do the work for you. Once the flight is found, the user merely has to confirm payment. Agentic AI can also be used in corporate settings. For instance, an e-commerce company can leverage agentic AI to conduct refunds. With clear rules, the AI system can decide whether a refund is allowed, process it automatically, update the in-house database, and create a shipping label. Agentic AI can even help financial companies to scan for fraud, automate loan approvals, and handle compliance checks. ****Meta Launches “Muse” Personal AI Assistant**** On September 8th,tech giant**Meta Platforms (**META**)** launched “Muse”, its first personal AI agent. Muse uses built-in intelligence to browse the internet and connect users to their favorite applications, like travel website **Expedia (**EXPE**)** or Google’s Gmail. ****Muse Dethrones ChatGPT**** Over the past few months, the number of AI product launches has been dizzying as tech companies look to cash in on the hype surrounding Wall Street’s hottest industry, artificial intelligence. In September alone, OpenAI expanded the “GPT-6” universe, Anthropic released “Claude Opus 5.5,” xAI launched “Grok 4.7,” and Google updated its family of applications. However, Meta’s “Muse” launch is arguably the most significant application release thus far in the AI revolution. In fact, within just a handful of days, Muse jumped to #1 on the **Apple (**AAPL**)** App Store and Google Play. Meanwhile, according to Apptopia app analytics, Meta reached 1.1 million installs roughly 10 days after launch, surpassing ChatGPT’s 2022 launch. For context, before the Muse launch, ChatGPT was the fastest-growing consumer application in history. ![Zacks Investment Research](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/image/zacks:44b4a585a094b-c6bb41c21bad2889386b2bc41ecf4a93-resized.webp) ****Mark Zuckerberg is Vindicated**** The business community widely recognizes Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg for his high-stakes, forward-looking business strategy. Zuck’s business acumen perfectly embodies hockey legend Wayne Gretzky’s famous philosophy: *“Skate to where the puck is going to be, not where it has been.”*...

Open Source AI.content: UPDATED 20:46 EDT / OCTOBER 05 2026 ### Reflection AI debuts open-source Beam model with 501B parameters Reflection AI Inc. today introduced Beam, an open-source large language model with 501 billion parameters. The launch comes a few months after the startup raised funding at a $25 billion valuation. Around the same time, Reflection AI reportedly inked a $6.3 billion deal with SpaceX Corp. to rent Nvidia GB300 NVL72 appliances. It used those systems, which each contain 72 graphics cards, to train Beam. Reflection AI benchmarked its model against GLM-5.2, an open-source LLM that includes about 250 billion more parameters. The company determined that Beam can perform some tasks better while using between one third and one fourth the hardware. Furthermore, it says that the LLM approaches the performance of Qwen 3.8-Max, a model with over 2 trillion parameters. The launch is particularly notable because many of the open-source ecosystem’s most advanced LLMs were created by Chinese companies. That includes Qwen 3.8-Max and GLM-5.2. Beam is the first open-source model from a U.S. startup to have demonstrated comparable or better performance. However, free LLMs continue to trail frontier models such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5.1. Reflection AI kicked off the development of Beam by training a relatively small prototype model. It then created a series of successively larger, more capable algorithms. The workflow eventually produced Beam Base, the foundation on which Beam is based. Reflection AI developed Beam Base using a cluster of 6,144 graphics cards. It trained the model on 23.8 trillion tokens sourced from the public web and commercial sources. According to Reflection AI, that dataset included a significant amount of software code. The company created custom filters for each programming language to remove low-quality files. Reflection AI developed Beam Base in under four weeks. It subsequently performed midtraining, an optimization process that extended the model’s context window and enhanced its reasoning capabilities. That phase of the project set the stage for the third, most hardware-intensive phase of the training workflow. Reflection AI spun up 10,000 GB300 graphics cards and used them to launch 1.3 billion reinforcement learning sandboxes. Those are virtual environments in which an AI model learns new skills. Beam’s sandboxes were optimized for tasks such as generating code, searching the web and running AI agents. Reflection AI says that the project’s reinforcement learning phase took only four weeks. The company avoided unnecessary delays by developing software that prevented malfunctions from interrupting the workflow. According to Reflection AI, its cluster achieved a median recovery time of eight minutes across the 71 errors that cropped up during training. Beam is initially available through an early access program. Reflection AI plans to release its weights, documentation and fine-tuning tools later this month. ##### Photo of Reflection AI founders Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou: Lightspeed # A message from John Furrier, co-founder of SiliconANGLE: Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. Open Source AI.content: © 2026 Cybernews – Latest Cybersecurity and Tech News, Research & Analysis. # Germany’s sovereign AI model Kolibri challenges US and Chinese rivals Built in Germany from scratch. ![The logo of Kolibri and German flag between 2 green cabinets with drawers](https://media.cybernews.com/images/featured-big/2026/10/germany-kolibri-model.jpg) Image by Insaanu Studio via Unsplash/Illustration by Cybernews ![Eglė Krištopaitytė](data:image/svg+xml;charset%3D'utf-8',%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%2040%2040'%2F%3E) ![](/images/follow-us/google-g.png) Key Takeaways by [nexos.ai](https://nexos.ai), reviewed by Cybernews staff. **The new open-weight large language model (LLM), designed for public administration, is outperforming competitors from Alibaba and Nvidia.** The Heidelberg-based AI startup Aleph Alpha released Kolibri on October 3rd, 2026, which is German Unity Day. Kolibri is an English-German Mixture-of-Experts Transformer, meaning it is divided into separate sub-networks called “experts.” The model uses 3.46 billion active parameters per token, out of 78.1B total. The model was specifically built for “sovereign mission-critical work” in regulated areas, including public administration, industrials, and aerospace, taking into account their particular “domain-specific language, regulatory, and procedural realities.” ## More from Cybernews ![A mascot for Meta's AI agent Muse](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/meta-muse-privacy.jpg) ![claude-logo-getty](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/03/claude.jpg) ![Anthropic logo](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/03/claude-pentagon.jpg) ![Ray-Ban Meta glasses](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/07/RaybamAIglasses.jpg) ![arXiv AI](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/shutterstock_2400385601.jpg) ![Tavus HIM model Griffin](https://media.cybernews.com/images/thumbnail/2026/10/tavus_griffin.gif) The company says Kolibri’s small, efficient size allows it to run on-premises without sending internal data to third-party inference services. Kolibri complies with the EU AI Act, the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), according to Aleph Alpha, with “copyright law being a focus of our work to trustworthy technology.” The model was built in Germany and trained on infrastructure in Germany and Finland, under the law of these countries. It was specifically trained to answer “I don’t know” when it cannot provide an answer, reducing the risk of hallucinations. [Kolibri was developed as a German and English bilingual model](https://aleph-alpha.com/en/blog/kolibri-has-landed-a-sovereign-open-weight-model/), including organic German data – 21.3% of the pre-training tokens are German. “We started the year with the conviction that Europe needs its own sovereign AI. Built in Germany from scratch and on infrastructure in Europe specifically for our customers,” Aleph Alpha’s X post reads. ## Kolibri vs American and Chinese models Aleph Alpha compared Kolibri to 3 other open-weight models with up to 4 times its active parameter count: Alibaba’s Qwen 3.6-35B-A3B, Mistral Small 4 119B-A6B, and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B. Kolibri outperformed all rivals across mathematical reasoning in both German and English (AIME 2025 and 2026 benchmark), deep reasoning (GPQA diamond), and code (LiveCodeBench v6). The model also showed superiority across benchmarks assessing an AI agent’s ability to find and navigate through large amounts of information. Kolibri, however, fell behind Qwen’s 3.6-35B-A3B across long-context comprehension and retrieval. ## Where to download Kolibri? Open Source AI.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Running a 125B-Parameter LLM on a Home PC: "Strata" Opens a New Frontier for Local AI [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Strata, an AI execution application released on GitHub, enables a quantized version of the 125-billion-parameter "Qwen3.8-Flash-Next" model to run on consumer-grade high-end gaming PCs. By loading the entire Mixture of Experts (MoE) model into system RAM while placing only frequently used expert models in GPU VRAM, combined with speculative decoding, the software operates with just 12GB of VRAM and 32GB of RAM. On an RTX 5070 setup, the 2-bit quantized version achieved 94 tokens per second. Strata exposes an OpenAI-compatible API on localhost, allowing existing tools to connect without modification, though degraded output quality has been reported with low-bit quantization. ##### Key Elements ![Running a 125B-Parameter LLM on a Home PC: ](https://img.biggo.com/YJjHhrfBMJ-Z7p_1apznIUsM4xcHiaGqLBDwLj1CaKs/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzM2NGIyMDFhLWJkMzQtNDE0Ny04MDZhLTExMGUwMTIxNmI4M18xNzkxMjA3MDM4X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) As large language models (LLMs) continue to improve in capability, an effort to overturn the assumption that running cutting-edge models requires data-center-class compute resources is drawing attention. Strata, an AI execution application released on GitHub, is software that enables a quantized version of the 125-billion-parameter "Qwen3.8-Flash-Next" model to run locally at high speed on relatively accessible high-end gaming PCs. Strata, published by developer Niko1221, employs a design that loads the entire MoE (Mixture of Experts) model into system RAM while placing only the most frequently used expert models into GPU VRAM. By combining this with speculative decoding—where a lightweight model predicts the next token—it enables large-scale models to run even on PCs with limited VRAM capacity. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is composed of 24,576 small expert models, of which only 10 are needed to generate each token. Strata treats VRAM as an effective cache, with the roughly 29GB lookup table stored on an SSD and accessed as needed. ### System Requirements and Measured Performance Running Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with Strata requires an NVIDIA or AMD GPU with at least 12GB of VRAM, 32GB or more of RAM, 80GB or more of storage (SSD recommended), and Windows 10/11 or Linux. With 32GB of RAM, only the lightweight "Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GSQ-RCO Coder" variant—which omits expert models for non-coding tasks—can be executed. With 64GB of RAM, the 2-bit quantized "IQ2\_XS" and 3-bit quantized "IQ3\_XXS" and "IQ3\_S" versions will run, and higher-precision quantized versions can be selected with more RAM. In actual performance reports, the 2-bit quantized "Q2\_0" version ran at 94 tokens per second and the 3-bit quantized "IQ3\_S" version at 53 tokens per second on a system with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 (12GB VRAM), Ryzen 5 7600, and 64GB of RAM. Open Source AI.content: # Kolibri, a sovereign AI model built for free and for mission-critical national tasks, is open source and transparent in its development process, intended for use in regulated fields such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/00_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/00.png) German AI startup Aleph Alpha announced a new language model called ' **Kolibri** ' on October 3, 2026, which is German Unity Day. **Kolibri Has Landed: A Sovereign Open-Weight Model — Aleph Alpha** <https://aleph-alpha.com/en/blog/kolibri-has-landed-a-sovereign-open-weight-model/> One of Kolibri's key features is its efficient design, which limits the number of active parameters to 3 billion despite having a total of 78 billion parameters. At the time of its announcement, it supports English and German and context lengths of up to 1 million tokens. Furthermore, its sophisticated training pipeline automates the entire process from data ingestion, curation, ablation, pre-training, post-training, and final evaluation, enabling hundreds of experiments and stable pre-training without manual intervention even in the event of hardware failures or data connectivity issues. Kolibri is intended for use in highly regulated and mission-critical sectors such as public administration, industry, and aerospace, and it excels particularly in German language processing capabilities, reasoning, mathematics, agent behavior, and features optimized for customer-specific use cases. Kolibri optimizes the trade-off between model performance and deployment cost by using only 3 billion active parameters out of a total of 78 billion parameters for each token processing. The graph below shows the processing performance of various open models in English and German. The horizontal axis represents processing speed, and the vertical axis represents the benchmark score. In both English and German, Kolibri has secured the position of 'highest performance compared to models with the same speed.' [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/01_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/01.png) Benchmark results show Kolibri performing comparably to models with up to four times the number of active parameters, such as Nemotron 3 Super, in mathematical, coding, grounding, and long-text context tasks. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/02_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/06/kolibri/02.png) Regarding sovereignty and compliance considerations, Aleph Alpha defines 'sovereignty' from two perspectives: 'how the model is built' and 'how it is transferred to the customer.' Regarding model construction, they prioritize transparency in weighting and curation, making the decision-making process behind development visible, and explaining how the model arrived at a specific answer through its inference trajectory. Furthermore, Aleph Alpha's proprietary Merlin-Arthur protocol ensures model reliability, so Kolibri refrains from answering and reduces hallucination if the context does not support the answer. The model is built in Germany, and training is conducted without foreign control throughout the entire pipeline, from data curation to pre- and post-training and optimization in the model factory, on German and Finnish infrastructure, in accordance with European and German law. This end-to-end pipeline management is the foundation supporting model sovereignty, and by transferring management rights to the customer, they gain complete deployment flexibility and enable controllable inference processing to trade off cost and latency with answer quality.
