Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#start-of-content) [Skip to sidebar](#sidebar) / [Blog](https://github.blog/) [Try GitHub Copilot app](https://github.com/features/ai/github-app?utm_source=blog-header-button-cta&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=github-app-cli-Q1-push) [Attend GitHub Universe](https://githubuniverse.com/?utm_source=Blog-button&utm_medium=GitHub&utm_campaign=blog_button_seb_uni_26) [Home](https://github.blog/) / [AI & ML](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/) / [GitHub Copilot](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/) # ReviewBench: An open benchmark for AI code review We’re launching ReviewBench, a benchmark for code review agents built on representative GitHub pull requests, multi-source ground truth, calibrated evaluation, and production-aligned metrics. ![Geometric blocks featuring the GitHub invertocat logo and a web icon in a decorative background.](https://github.blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/generic-invertocat-logo.png?resize=1600%2C850) [Michelle Zhou](https://github.blog/author/miichellezhou/ "Posts by Michelle Zhou") & [Alejandro Carderera de Diego](https://github.blog/author/alejandrocarderera/ "Posts by Alejandro Carderera de Diego") | 11 minutes * Share: Agentic code review is becoming an essential piece of how development happens. It helps you inspect pull requests, catch issues, and decide what deserves attention before code ships. But the quality of existing AI reviewers can be hard to measure, and you need to know the strengths of a reviewer before you know if it will help you. Some reviewers surface more issues, some produce less noise, and some are stronger at catching critical problems while others surface smaller improvements, too. You may need code review to do different things within your workflow. That makes it important to understand how reviewers actually compare: what different systems catch, what they miss, and the tradeoffs they make. A good code review benchmark should reflect the diversity of real pull requests, capture a broad set of review findings, and support meaningful breakdowns by severity, category, and precision-recall preferences. For teams building code review agents, the benchmark should also provide an offline signal that reliably tracks whether changes are likely to improve the experience in production. Existing benchmarks often make tradeoffs between label quality, coverage, and how well they represent real-world code review, leaving a gap for a rigorous and reproducible evaluation methodology that brings these pieces together. We built [**ReviewBench**](https://review-bench.ai/)**, a new code review offline benchmark**, to address that gap, and it is available for you to use today. It follows the language, repo size, and size distribution of pull requests, modeled after over 100 million real pull requests on GitHub. It uses a multi-source golden set and a consistent evaluation rubric and has been independently validated by senior engineers. Just as important, with the help of ReviewBench, our offline evaluation of Copilot code review (CCR) has become more effective at anticipating the direction of production experiments, giving us greater confidence that measured improvements reflect meaningful gains for users. In this post, we’ll walk through how ReviewBench is constructed, how it establishes reliable ground truth and scoring, and how to onboard your own code review system and submit results. ## ReviewBench at a glance 1 ### What we built A realistic, comprehensive benchmark for AI code review agents 103.9M ### GitHub pull requests Analyze distributions by language, repository size, and change shape. ### Representative benchmark corpus 219 public pull requests across 19 languages, aligned to GitHub-wide distributions while preserving substantive review cases. ### Multi-source golden set * Human reviewers * Frontier LLMs * Static analysis ### Structured findings Every finding is labeled for severity and category, enabling user-tailored slices. #### Severity * Critical * Medium * Lo...

Infra & Chips.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Nvidia's $20 Billion Groq Deal Draws Shareholder Lawsuit From Former Engineers [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Two former Groq engineers have filed a lawsuit in Delaware's Court of Chancery alleging that Nvidia's $20 billion asset deal with the AI chip startup unfairly squeezed out common stockholders. The complaint claims Groq's board approved the transaction without a required stockholder vote and that $17 billion of the deal value went to a non-exclusive technology license while another $3 billion was reserved for employee stock awards. Groq has called the lawsuit meritless and said it will defend itself vigorously. Nvidia has not commented on the litigation. ##### Key Elements ![Nvidia's $20 Billion Groq Deal Draws Shareholder Lawsuit From Former Engineers](https://img.biggo.com/0wAiLEjI8NkcbWSTvFfEa_460KUCeiIqgozG7i8w6OM/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwL2NjMGJlMGFlLWY3ZmQtNDFjZC1iNjU3LWYzMWQ0YWExZjVmM18xNzkxMjUxMTA0X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) is facing a legal challenge over its $20 billion asset agreement with AI chip designer Groq, after two former engineers at the startup alleged that stockholders were squeezed out at an unfairly low price. Joshua Rubin and Benjamin Serebrin filed the complaint on Oct. 2 in Delaware's Court of Chancery. Both had departed Groq before the Nvidia transaction was announced, according to their LinkedIn profiles, but the lawsuit states they continued to hold equity in the company. The case marks the first significant legal test of a deal structure that has drawn scrutiny for how it allocates value between technology licenses, employee compensation, and common stockholders. The dispute traces back to a December licensing agreement that granted Nvidia access to Groq's inference technology, which is used to run trained AI models efficiently. As part of that arrangement, Groq founder and CEO Jonathan Ross and President Sunny Madra joined Nvidia, along with other senior executives. The lawsuit indicates that roughly 150 to 200 Groq engineers also became Nvidia employees in connection with the transaction. Groq, for its part, has maintained that it will continue operating as an independent company and has raised approximately $1 billion since June from investors that include Nvidia itself. The core of the complaint centers on how the $20 billion was divided. The plaintiffs allege that Nvidia assigned $17 billion to a license described as non-exclusive, while another $3 billion was reserved in Nvidia restricted stock units for Groq employees who moved with the technology. The lawsuit further claims that investment funds with representatives on Groq's board were positioned to capture windfall returns from what the plaintiffs describe as a later squeeze-out transaction. "A Board majority was conflicted as a result," the complaint states, adding that "the Board's conflicted choice cost Groq's stockholders billions of dollars." The former engineers argue that Groq's directors "sold the company to Nvidia without the stockholder vote Delaware law requires and without any process designed to test or maximize the value of what Nvidia bought." Groq has forcefully rejected the allegations. A company spokesperson said the licensing agreement "delivered exceptional value for Groq, our investors, and our employees." The spokesperson added that the lawsuit "is meritless and we will vigorously defend ourselves against it," while emphasizing that the company remains focused on serving customers and building what it describes as the world's leading AI inference cloud. Nvidia Is Becoming an Inference Fight, Not a Chip Fight The next big AI chip battle may not be about who trains the biggest model. It could be about who can make [AI respond fastest](https://www.benzinga.com/markets/tech/26/10/62118140/ai-stocks-bubble-earnings) once the model is already built. That is putting **Cerebras Systems Inc.** [(NASDAQ:](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/CBRS)[CBRS](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/CBRS)) and **Nvidia Corp** [(NASDAQ:](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/NVDA)[NVDA](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/NVDA)) on opposite sides of an increasingly valuable fight over AI inference. ## Altman Reassures Cerebras Investors Cerebras shares climbed more than 7% in early trading Monday after **OpenAI** CEO **Sam Altman** pushed back against speculation that the chipmaker had lost a key role at OpenAI. "Cerebras is a close partner, and we have a deep engagement pushing on the frontiers of speed," Altman [said](https://x.com/sama/status/2106147184693620924?s=20) in a post on X. The comments came days after Cerebras shares fell nearly 20% after a SemiAnalysis [report](https://lnkd.in/p/gU9ai9Z2) said OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast tier ran on Nvidia GPUs rather than Cerebras hardware. The report raised an obvious question for investors: If OpenAI is turning to Nvidia for its fastest AI experience, where does that leave Cerebras? The answer may be more nuanced than a single model or a single customer deployment. OpenAI and Cerebras announced a multiyear agreement in January for 750 megawatts of Cerebras inference capacity through 2028. OpenAI said at the time that Cerebras would add a dedicated low-latency solution to its compute portfolio, with the goal of delivering faster responses across workloads. ## Speed Is Becoming a Market That distinction matters because inference is what happens after an AI model has been trained: It is the computing required every time a user asks a question, generates code or interacts with an AI agent. Cerebras has built its investment case around making that process faster. The company said in August that its cloud business grew 281% year over year, while data-center capacity live or under contract surpassed 600 megawatts. It also said manufacturing capacity was set to increase more than 10 times in 2026. Now Wall Street is putting a number behind that opportunity. Mizuho analyst Vijay Rakesh estimates the fast-inference market could reach $550 billion by 2030, representing roughly 20% of AI workloads. He reiterated an Outperform rating and [$300 price target](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/CBRS/price-targets) on CBRS Monday. It lies in rethinking the systems that make up the server rooms, by [Gianni Rusconi](https://argomenti.ilsole24ore.com/gianni-rusconi.html) [![](/static/img/icon-google--g.svg)Aggiungi Il Sole 24 Ore ai preferiti su Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=ilsole24ore.com) 6' min read Translated by AI For feedback, please contact [english@ilsole24ore.com](mailto:english@ilsole24ore.com?body=https://en.ilsole24ore.com/art/data-centres-what-they-are-like-today-and-what-they-will-be-like-in-five-years-time-AJ3MWHZB) [Versione italiana](https://www.ilsole24ore.com/art/i-data-center-l-ai-come-sono-oggi-e-come-saranno-cinque-anni-AJ3MWHZB) 6' min read Translated by AI For feedback, please contact [english@ilsole24ore.com](mailto:english@ilsole24ore.com?body=https://en.ilsole24ore.com/art/data-centres-what-they-are-like-today-and-what-they-will-be-like-in-five-years-time-AJ3MWHZB) [Versione italiana](https://www.ilsole24ore.com/art/i-data-center-l-ai-come-sono-oggi-e-come-saranno-cinque-anni-AJ3MWHZB) ZAGREB – Artificial intelligence is reshaping data centres, and this process of change ranges from rack density to the systems that supply power and dissipate heat. The issue is well known: infrastructure is required to support heavier workloads and ensure ever-faster processing cycles, whilst projects involving the use of AI are growing in scale. Part of the solution is built in the factory, whilst other aspects concern technologies for cooling and controlling the systems, with liquid-cooling solutions and digital tools becoming increasingly prevalent. Amazon could collect billions of dollars for AI chips and continue using those same chips to serve customers. That is the logic behind a reported proposal to transfer approximately $8 billion of Nvidia hardware to an investment vehicle then lease it back. The attraction is immediate cash. The price is a stream of future payments whose terms will determine whether the transaction creates value. Let’s break down what has been reported, why Amazon would consider this financing structure and how to assess the economics beyond the headline. We’ll examine its cash flow, AWS profitability, GPU rental prices and valuation before considering the implications for US and Indian investors. Our assessment is that the proposal is understandable in a period of exceptional infrastructure spending. Its financial merit depends on the cash actually released, the cost of continued access and the risks Amazon retains. As of October 5, the public reporting describes discussions rather than a completed transaction. ## **What is Amazon’s proposed $8 billion Nvidia deal?** The Financial Times reported the proposal on October 2. Reuters subsequently reported that Amazon had been discussing investor interest in a special-purpose vehicle (SPV) that would hold thousands of Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips. Amazon would lease the hardware back while the vehicle raised outside financing. An SPV is a separate legal entity created for a defined transaction. Here, its purpose would be to connect investors supplying capital with equipment that Amazon continues to use.
